blocks.title: Ionic bonding
blocks.md: Atoms bond to get a **full outer shell**. In **ionic bonding** a **metal** atom **gives** electrons to a **non-metal** atom. The metal forms a **positive ion** (cation) and the non-metal a **negative ion** (anion): Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The oppositely charged ions attract strongly in a **giant lattice**. Formulae come from charges: Na⁺Cl⁻ → NaCl; Mg²⁺O²⁻ → MgO; Ca²⁺ with two Cl⁻ → CaCl₂.

items.text: metal atom gives an electron to a non-metal atom: ions attract

blocks.caption: Ionic bonding in sodium chloride.
blocks.alt: A sodium atom giving one electron to a chlorine atom, forming a sodium ion and a chloride ion, each with a full outer shell.

blocks.title: Covalent bonding
blocks.md: In **covalent bonding** two **non-metal** atoms **share pairs of electrons**. Examples: hydrogen H₂ (1 pair), chlorine Cl₂ (1), water H₂O (2 pairs), ammonia NH₃, methane CH₄, oxygen O₂ (a **double bond**, 2 pairs) and nitrogen N₂ (a **triple bond**, 3 pairs), carbon dioxide CO₂ (two double bonds). Most covalent substances form separate **molecules**.

items.text: each O–H bond = one shared pair

blocks.caption: A water molecule: oxygen shares one pair of electrons with each hydrogen.
blocks.alt: An oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, with the note that each O-H bond is a shared pair of electrons.

blocks.title: Bonding and properties
blocks.md: **Ionic compounds**: high melting points, hard but brittle, **conduct electricity when molten or dissolved** (ions move) but not as solids. **Simple molecular compounds**: low melting and boiling points, **do not conduct**. **Giant covalent structures** (diamond, graphite, silica): very high melting points; diamond is very hard; **graphite** is soft and conducts. **Metals**: positive ions in a sea of free electrons; they conduct and are malleable.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Ionic solids do not conduct because their ions cannot move; they conduct when melted or in solution.
- Covalent does not mean weak: the bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the forces **between** molecules are weak.
- Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, not to 'become happy'.

blocks.statement: Write the formula of aluminium oxide (Al³⁺ and O²⁻).
steps: Cross over the charges: Al gets 2, O gets 3.

blocks.title: Explain conductivity
blocks.statement: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct but molten sodium chloride does?
steps: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.
When molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
blocks.answer: The ions can move only when molten or dissolved.

blocks.title: Writing a formula
blocks.md: Valencies (combining powers): **H, Na, K, Ag, Cl, OH, NO₃ = 1**; **Mg, Ca, Zn, Cu(II), O, S, CO₃, SO₄ = 2**; **Al = 3** (iron is 2 in iron(II), 3 in iron(III)). **Cross over** the valencies and simplify: magnesium chloride Mg(2) Cl(1) → MgCl₂; aluminium oxide Al(3) O(2) → Al₂O₃; calcium hydroxide Ca(2) OH(1) → Ca(OH)₂; aluminium sulphate Al(3) SO₄(2) → Al₂(SO₄)₃. Use a **bracket** if more than one of a group is needed.

items.text: 4 H and 2 O on each side: the equation is balanced

blocks.caption: A balanced equation shown with particles.
blocks.alt: Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule on the left, an arrow, and two water molecules on the right, with the note that there are 4 H and 2 O on each side.

blocks.title: Balancing equations
blocks.md: A **word equation** names reactants and products: *magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide*. In a **balanced symbol equation** the number of atoms of each element is the **same on both sides** because atoms are not created or destroyed. Steps: (1) write correct formulae; (2) count atoms; (3) change **coefficients** (big numbers in front), **never the subscripts**; (4) recount. Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO and 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.

blocks.title: State symbols and examples
blocks.md: **(s)** solid, **(l)** liquid, **(g)** gas, **(aq)** aqueous (dissolved in water). Examples: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g); CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (heating limestone); Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (making iron).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Never change a subscript to balance an equation: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water.
- Balance one element at a time and recount all the others.
- A bracket multiplies everything inside it: Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O and 2 H.

blocks.title: Balance an equation
steps: Oxygen: 3 O₂ gives 6 O, and 2 Al₂O₃ also gives 6 O.
Then Al: 2 Al₂O₃ has 4 Al, so write 4 Al: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.

blocks.title: Formula of aluminium sulphate
blocks.statement: Write the formula of aluminium sulphate (Al³⁺, SO₄²⁻).
steps: Cross over: Al gets 2, SO₄ gets 3.
Brackets are needed for SO₄: Al₂(SO₄)₃.
